title: Engineering Context for SOC Agents: Lessons, Failures, and Open Questions
thesis: Context for SOC agents (runbooks, skills, system prompts) must be measured by ablation and evaluated across models and harnesses, because hand-tuned or even automatically evolved context overfits its original model and harness and may be neutral or harmful on newer frontier models.
summary: Dan Dye, a Google Cloud Security engineer, gives an in-the-trenches account of building context for security operations agents. He started with Markdown AI runbooks and persona sub-agents on a local Cline harness, moved to Google's agent development kit with multi-agent delegation, and then found that platform knowledge bases now accept native Markdown in Drive. He sketches that context work briefly, then turns to what he calls the real problem: new frontier models arrive weekly, so he asks whether his skills help or hurt, and whether they will be in the next model's pre-training. He frames a skills ablation, 'does a skill earn its tokens?', and shows a table comparing prompt-only, monolithic runbooks, graph workflows and progressive-disclosure variants on one malware case. He says that embedding the grading rubric inside the runbooks contaminated later experiments. Evolving skills with GEPA looked like a miracle (99.8% lower simulated loss, 26.6% fewer tokens, 21.2% lower latency), but the gains vanished on another model or harness; he lists four failure modes such as literal environment-variable placeholders and Mermaid diagrams. On newer frontier models a threat-hunting benchmark showed no runbook scoring above his raw runbook, while newer harness-evolution frameworks (Harness squared) recovered nearly saturating scores. He closes by releasing a repo to deploy and benchmark open-weight Gemma and other models on Google Cloud, with GPU cost tables and an idle-GPU shutdown agent, and Q&A covers verbosity-biased judges, descriptive versus prescriptive skills, and whether sub-agents still pay off.
argument: Context engineering for SOC agents now includes mixed knowledge bases, skills, runbooks and system prompts, but the weekly cadence of frontier models means each piece may become unnecessary or harmful.
Advice to simply delete prompts and see what happens is not scientific; a skill ablation that asks whether a skill earns its tokens is needed, with measured scores and token counts.
Convenience shortcuts such as embedding the rubric in the runbook can make agents complete tasks but contaminate evolution experiments and inflate results.

Automated skill evolution (GEPA) produced dramatic in-harness gains that did not transfer, because the evolved context overfit the model and harness (placeholders, harness-specific pseudo-tools, diagram bloat, brittle branches).

Newer harness-evolution methods and open-weight models give new ways to test and regularize skills across harnesses and model sizes, but evaluations for blue-team work saturate and need to get harder and more complete.
As models improve, procedural workflows may collapse toward deterministic code or SOAR playbooks, with agents used to author them rather than reason through repeated tasks.

claims.claim: Agent knowledge bases are shifting from self-configured vector stores and RAG to platform-managed connectors, and a corpus can now be native Markdown documents in a Drive folder that agents create, read, update, delete and comment on.
claims.evidence: Cited a recent Drive and Docs release note (Oct 5, 2026) and an ADK Docs comment-assistant post; he has experiments in an ADK repo.

claims.claim: On one Lokibot C2 malware case, prompt-only context used about 4.92M tokens and scored 75 (C), monolithic runbooks 1.88M tokens and 95 (A), ADK graph workflows 0.87M and 100, skills progressive disclosure 285K and 95, and dual progressive disclosure (skills plus MCP) 113K and 95.
claims.evidence: Skills-ablation table on a slide for Experiment 1; the first two versions are the ablation baseline; judging was LLM-as-judge with rubrics and letter grades.

claims.claim: The ablation was run on four cases, not one: across Lokibot C2 (case 33279), Compromised User IRP (case 33284), a Honeytoken Rule alert and an AvosLocker triage alert, prompt-only used 4.2M to 4.9M tokens with scores of 70 to 75 (C range), while skills progressive disclosure and dual progressive disclosure used 250K to 313K and 99K to 125K tokens and scored 93 to 95; ADK graph workflows used about 870K tokens and scored 90 to 100.
claims.evidence: adk_runbooks graph-workflows overview table on a slide, with three further percentage-reduction columns (-60.2% to -60.5%, -94.0% to -97.1%, -97.0% to -98.0%) whose headers are off frame.

claims.claim: Embedding the grading rubric directly in skills and runbooks kept agents on task and completing steps, but it gave the LLM the answer to the test and seriously contaminated later evolution experiments.
claims.evidence: The speaker's own account of his evaluation setup.

claims.claim: GEPA evolution of four SOC runbooks with Gemini 2.5 Pro reflecting and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite as the agent model cut simulated breach loss 99.8% ($250,051 to $101), total tokens 26.6% (529k to 388k) and mean triage latency 21.2% (40.5 s to 31.9 s).
claims.evidence: Slide titled 'In-Harness GEPA Looked Like a Miracle'.

claims.claim: The evolved improvements disappeared when tested on a different model or harness: evolving the harness works but does not transfer, as the changes overfit.
claims.evidence: His experiments; four named failure modes on a slide; he cites a paper stating evolved harnesses overfit the benchmark.

claims.claim: When the exact GEPA-evolved runbooks were transferred to the interactive Harbor soc-cli sandbox (90 trials), they lost to the clean human-written skill on every model: gemini-3.5-flash-lite 0.841 (90% pass, $5 simulated loss) to 0.746 (60%, $6.5k), -11.3%; gemini-2.5-flash 0.856 (90%, $505) to 0.703 (60%, $1.0k), -17.8%; gemini-2.5-flash-lite 0.655 (50%, $5.5k) to 0.436 (10%, $11.0k), -33.4%.
claims.evidence: Slide 'Harbor Sandbox Collapse' with a transfer-delta column and a footer 'Evolved runbooks lost to the human baseline on every model, open-model-deploy-gcp PR #14'.

claims.claim: Four things failed to transfer: literal ${VAR_NAME} placeholders copied into CLI flags by smaller models, harness-specific pseudo-tools (ask_followup_question, attempt_completion) invoked in headless containers, 3,648 words and 55-line Mermaid sequenceDiagrams that diluted instruction attention on Flash-Lite, and nested IF/ELSE branches that caused PREMATURE_TERMINATION_ZERO_TOOLS.
claims.evidence: Slide 'Why Evolved Runbooks Failed to Transfer'; speaker added that he had championed Mermaid diagrams as human and machine readable.

claims.claim: On a proactive threat-hunting benchmark (48 trajectories across 3 models and 4 runbook arms) a no-runbook arm scored mean hunt composite 0.8554 and Harbor 0.8673, above his raw hunt runbook at 0.8295 and 0.8575, with identical 92% verdict accuracy, 56% 168-hour widening rate and 100% LOLBin-safe rate.
claims.evidence: Scorecard table in his open-model-deploy-gcp repo, shown with the first two rows highlighted; speaker said some newest models confirmed the bitter lesson and his handcrafted skills were harmful.

claims.claim: The Harness squared evolution framework picked the right direction and nearly saturated the threat-hunting runbook evaluation: its evolved hunt runbook scored mean hunt composite 0.9813 and Harbor 0.9587 with 100% verdict accuracy, 168-hour widening and LOLBin-safe rates, versus 0.9510 and 0.9337 for a compressed track-B runbook, and 0.8554 for no runbook; he says this shows blue-team evals need to be harder.
claims.evidence: Full four-arm scorecard table in the open-model-deploy-gcp README (48 trajectories across 3 models and 4 arms).

claims.claim: Open-weight models can be used as proxies for older frontier models to test and retest skills at different sizes; the closed gemini-3.5-flash-lite nearly saturates the tests and tops the leaderboard (100% pass, 5 of 5, rubric 97.0, 11.36 s) ahead of gemma-3-12b-it (60%, 91.0), gemma-4-e4b-it (80%, 91.0), qwen3.8-27b (60%, 88.4) and llama-3.1-nemotron-70b-instruct (60%, 86.0), and score and tokens per second vary with model revision and size.
claims.evidence: His hypothesis, a public repo with deployment recipes, a GPU cost table (for example gemma-4-e2b on one L4 at $0.70/hr, gemma-4-31b on two A100s at $7.34/hr) and a leaderboard table on a slide; pass rates are on a 5-case run of a 10-case Tier 1 suite.

claims.claim: Padding a skill with meandering but not factually wrong text improved his evaluation score, apparently because the LLM judge was impressed by verbose output and keyed on string presence rather than output length.
claims.evidence: An accidental result of a test intended to degrade performance; explained by the agent in a follow-up chat; no numbers shown.

claims.claim: Skills compressed with Simplified Technical English gave a small lift in his evaluation.
claims.evidence: Mentioned as part of the same experiment; no numbers.

claims.claim: A single agent may now replace persona-driven sub-agents, and graph workflows are approaching a plain Python file or SOAR playbook that an agent writes once and then executes procedurally.
claims.evidence: Speculation in answer to a question; he has not evaluated the uplift of sub-agents against the base harness.

frameworks.name: Skills ablation: does a skill earn its tokens?
frameworks.description: Compare versions of the same task with the skill removed and present, tracking tokens and an LLM-judge score. His versions: A prompt-only, B monolithic runbooks, C ADK graph workflows, D skills progressive disclosure, E dual progressive disclosure (skills and MCP tools).

frameworks.name: Evolving improvements lineup
frameworks.description: GEPA (Genetic Pareto Prompt Evolution), DSPy, AQuA (Ambient Quality Agent) outer loop, Harness squared, RRSI (Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement, aimed at harness transfer), and Gemini Enterprise Eval Studio.

frameworks.name: Why evolved runbooks fail to transfer
frameworks.description: Four causes: placeholder syntax copied literally, harness-specific pseudo-tools, Mermaid and IF/ELSE bloat that dilutes instruction attention, and nested branches causing zero-tool premature termination.

frameworks.name: Ten best practices for agentic SOC runbooks
frameworks.description: Codified in docs/RUNBOOK_AUTHORING_BEST_PRACTICES.md and enforced in RunbookSafetyGuard (check_runbook_safety with strict_context_hygiene=True, max_words=350). Visible items: 1 hard 300 to 350 word budget (about 60% ordered investigation steps, 25% disposition and containment matrix, 15% output fields); 2 never include Mermaid diagrams in agent-consumed markdown; 3 never reference IDE pseudo-tools (ask_followup_question, attempt_completion, write_to_file), use deterministic conditional branches; 4 never use ${VAR_NAME} or placeholder template variables, name exact UDM or alert schema fields; 5 preserve all four mandatory disposition branches (escalate_incident, contain_and_patch, tune_detection, benign_or_inconclusive, the last two with zero destructive actions). Items 6 to 10 were not visible.

frameworks.name: idle_compute_guard pipeline
frameworks.description: Four stages: cloud telemetry (Idle Endpoint Guard, AI Usage Spike Guard, Cloud Billing Velocity alerts), a Cloud Pub/Sub event bus, an Antigravity SDK agent (parse_alert_notification routing idle, spike and billing alerts, running gemini-2.5-flash), and Vertex AI and SOAR tools (list_active_endpoints, undeploy_vertex_model, delete_vertex_endpoint, log_soar_remediation).

frameworks.name: Open-weight models as six-month-old frontier models
frameworks.description: Use a range of open-weight sizes and revisions as cheaper, older proxies to test whether skills transfer, with hardware, cost per hour and tokens per second as extra axes.

offense: Context overfitting: evolved skills tuned to one model and harness lose their gains or hurt elsewhere.
Rubric leakage: placing grading criteria in the runbook lets the agent target the test and contaminates evaluation.
LLM-judge verbosity bias: a longer, noisier skill raised the judge's score because longer outputs matched string checks.
Harness-specific artifacts: literal placeholder strings in CLI flags and calls to pseudo-tools that do not exist in headless containers.
Instruction dilution and brittle control flow: very long runbooks, Mermaid diagrams and nested IF/ELSE branches caused ignored instructions and premature termination with zero tool calls.
Operational failure modes: a root agent that does the work itself instead of delegating, tool-call infinite loops, and idle GPUs running up costs.
defense: Run skills ablations and report tokens and score per variant before adopting or keeping a skill; re-run when a new model lands.
Keep grading rubrics out of runbooks and prompts so evaluations are not contaminated.
Test evolved or hand-tuned context on at least one other model and harness, and across several open-weight sizes, before trusting a gain.
Use graph workflows to enforce multi-step tool trajectories and to cut tokens; use progressive disclosure for both skills and MCP tools.
Write human-readable skills that describe the task with the weakest sufficient theory rather than over-prescribing, and strip harness-specific syntax, Mermaid diagrams and nested branching.
Add judges and checks that measure output length and what was done, not only string matches; guard compute with idle-GPU detectors and tool-call loop limits.
takeaways: Before the next model upgrade, re-run your SOC agent skills with the skill removed; keep only those whose token cost is justified by a measured score gain.
Do not treat automated prompt or skill evolution results as real until they hold on a second model and harness; require a transfer test in your acceptance criteria.
Separate rubric and evaluation data from the agent's context, and check your LLM judges for verbosity and string-matching bias.
Plan for the workflows you run repeatedly to harden into deterministic playbooks, with agents used to author and update them.
Invest in harder, broader blue-team evals: the author's threat-hunt eval is nearly saturated and only about 15 of 50-plus runbooks are covered.
limits: The speaker framed the talk as an inquiry with open questions rather than answers, and said it does not advocate for Google's agent platform.
He has not evaluated whether multi-agent delegation still beats a single agent with the base harness.
Evaluations cover about 15 of 50-plus runbooks and he has not analyzed task complexity versus skill benefit.
Embedded rubrics contaminated his evolution experiments.
Which memories and enterprise context to inject for SOC agents (relevance selection) remains an open problem; he did not resolve how to choose which models to use from Model Garden.
Evaluation saturation: current blue-team evals are nearly saturated by newer methods.
critique: The ablation covers four cases with one score per variant and no repeat runs or variance; differences of 5 points on an LLM-judged letter grade should not be read as stable, though the token reductions are large and consistent across all four cases.

The headline GEPA gains are from simulated breach loss and a mean triage latency whose benchmark is not described; the speaker's later statement that rubrics were embedded in the runbooks and that the judge rewarded verbosity bears on all judge-based scores in the talk.

The threat-hunt result (no runbook 0.8554 vs raw runbook 0.8295) is a small difference with identical verdict accuracy and rates, and the speaker described the raw skills as harmful. The larger spread in the full table is between those two arms and the compressed and Harness-squared-evolved runbooks (0.9510 and 0.9813). The evolved arm is also the one the speaker describes as near-saturated, and the talk did not show whether it was tested on anything other than the benchmark it was evolved on, which is the overfitting risk he describes earlier.

The Harbor collapse table (90 trials over three models) is the largest non-transfer test shown, and it covers only Gemini-family models; transfer to other vendors' models or to other harnesses was not shown.
The leaderboard compares a closed hosted model with open models on dedicated GPUs over 5 cases, so pass rates move in 20-point steps and rank order below the leader rests on small differences.
The talk is largely about agent engineering methodology; detection quality and investigation accuracy against real incidents were not shown, and the eval environments are simulated.
Several recommendations (descriptive over prescriptive skills, weakest-theory principle) came from audience members and were agreed to rather than tested.

The 'open weights equal six-month-old frontier models' thesis was asserted and only partly tested; the question about how it held up was answered by pointing to skills that hurt benchmarks rather than a size-by-size result.
The repo and talk use Google Cloud tooling (ADK, Vertex AI, Gemini), and the speaker works at Google Cloud Security; he said the talk is an inquiry with open questions.
qa: Q: How has the hypothesis that open-weight models act like six-month-old frontier models held up? A: He saw some of his skills actively harming his benchmarks, which makes him question the work given the model release cadence, but he thinks it still matters: there is value at smaller sizes, and regularized skills improved at small sizes also work better in larger models.

He then described the meander-skill experiment: expecting a padded skill to degrade results, the evaluation improved, which the agent attributed to the LLM judge being impressed by verbosity and keying on strings.

Audience comment: descriptive skills transcend models while prescriptive ones degrade performance; the speaker agreed and tied it to a 'weakest theory/weakest hypothesis' principle (use just enough words to describe the task and give the model discretion).

Q: Did task complexity change whether skills helped? A: His first-generation evals measured tool-call trajectory across multi-step sessions, the evaluations changed through generations, and only about 15 of 50-plus runbooks are covered; a complexity analysis to find weak spots is a good idea he will write down.
Q: Did you try the RLM module in DSPy? A: No, but he will check it out.

Q: Did you evaluate the uplift of multi-agent systems over the plain harness with sub-agents? A: Not yet; delegation helped when context windows were small, but a single agent may now replace persona-driven sub-agents, though offloading to smaller, cheaper models is good, and mature graph workflows look like a SOAR playbook an agent writes once.

key_frames.caption: Skills ablation across four SOC cases: prompt-only 4.2M to 4.9M tokens at C grades versus progressive disclosure at 99K to 313K tokens and 93 to 95, with the architectural insights that explain it.
Harbor Sandbox Collapse: GEPA-evolved runbooks lose to the human skill on every model, from -11.3% to -33.4%, with pass rates falling from 90% to 60% and 50% to 10%.
Four reasons evolved runbooks failed to transfer: placeholders, harness-specific pseudo-tools, Mermaid and IF/ELSE bloat, and zero-tool termination.
Full threat-hunt scorecard: no runbook 0.8554 and raw runbook 0.8295 versus compressed 0.9510 and Harness-squared-evolved 0.9813 across 48 trajectories.
Open-weight leaderboard on the SOC Tier 1 suite: closed gemini-3.5-flash-lite at 100% and 97.0 versus Gemma, Qwen and Nemotron models at 60% to 80%, with latency and tokens per second.

signal.reason: A measurement-based account of context and skill evolution failing to transfer, with concrete numbers and failure modes; the evidence comes from one author's experiments in simulated environments.
